source_refs.note: Book p. 287: 11.1.2 Vector-Valued Function, r(t) = <f(t), g(t), h(t)> = f(t) i + g(t) j + h(t) k

blocks.text: A vector-valued function in a single variable is a function that takes one variable as input and returns a vector as output. Each component of the output vector is itself a scalar function of the input. Typically, a vector-valued function is written as:

blocks.latex: \begin{aligned}\mathbf{r}(t) &= \langle f(t), g(t), h(t)\rangle \\ &= f(t)\hat{i} + g(t)\hat{j} + h(t)\hat{k}\end{aligned}
blocks.text_alt: r of t equals the ordered triple f of t, g of t, h of t, which equals f of t times i plus g of t times j plus h of t times k

blocks.text: Where \(\hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k}\) are the unit vectors associated with the rectangular coordinates; \(f(t), g(t)\), and \(h(t)\) are scalar functions of \(t\), which are the components of the vector-valued function \(\mathbf{r}(t)\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Both forms say the same thing. \(\langle f(t), g(t), h(t)\rangle\) lists the three components in order (\(x\) first, then \(y\), then \(z\)); \(f(t)\hat{i} + g(t)\hat{j} + h(t)\hat{k}\) writes each component next to its unit vector.
In 2D there is no \(\hat{k}\) part: \(\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle f(t), g(t)\rangle = f(t)\hat{i} + g(t)\hat{j}\).
The important word is "single variable": all components depend on the SAME \(t\). One value of \(t\) fixes all components at once, so it fixes one vector.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Our illustration: for \(\mathbf{r}(t) = t\hat{i} + t^{2}\hat{j}\) (from the Introduction) the components are \(f(t) = t\) and \(g(t) = t^{2}\), two scalar functions. At \(t = 3\):
\[\mathbf{r}(3) = 3\hat{i} + 9\hat{j} = \langle 3, 9\rangle\]
One number went in, one vector came out.
The length of the vector, \(|\mathbf{r}(t)| = \sqrt{t^{2} + t^{4}}\), is again a scalar function of \(t\).

rows: Written in bold or with an arrow: \(\mathbf{r}(t)\)

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. A vector-valued function takes one variable \(t\) and returns a vector.
2. Each component \(f(t), g(t), h(t)\) is a scalar function of the same \(t\).
3. \(\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle f(t), g(t), h(t)\rangle = f(t)\hat{i} + g(t)\hat{j} + h(t)\hat{k}\); in 2D drop the \(\hat{k}\) part.
4. \(\hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k}\) are the unit vectors along the \(x\)-, \(y\)- and \(z\)-axes.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Adding the components: \(\langle t, t^{2}\rangle\) is a vector, not the number \(t + t^{2}\).
2. Changing the order: \(\langle f, g, h\rangle\) always means \(x\), then \(y\), then \(z\).
3. Using different variables in different components (one in \(t\), another in \(s\)): all components share one input \(t\).
